description: TERNARY is an independent initiative exploring the intersection of artificial intelligence, scientific computing, and space exploration. Led by a solo builder pursuing a Master of Science in Cybersecurity at NYU Tandon, the team focuses on developing innovative, data-driven solutions to complex scientific challenges. While participating independently, I welcome opportunities for technical exchange, mentorship, and collaboration with the broader aerospace research community.
summary:
ARCAUS — Fire Beyond Gravity -  is an interactive scientific research observatory I developed to make NASA’s microgravity combustion research more accessible, understandable, and actionable.
     Created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge *Flame in Freefall*, ARCAUS brings together evidence from NASA investigations, including BASS-II, Saffire-V, and SoFIE-GEL, to explore how materials, oxygen concentration, and airflow influence flame behavior in microgravity.
The platform organizes 31 curated scientific findings, presents five cross-study comparisons, and visualizes verified experimental data, including 18 PMMA flame-spread test runs and 27 fabric combustion records. Through interactive graphs, experiment exhibits, and source-linked evidence, researchers can explore patterns while distinguishing verified measurements, published conclusions, and scientific hypotheses.
     ARCAUS addresses the challenge of interpreting fragmented scientific research without overlooking differences in experimental conditions. Rather than predicting fire behavior, it helps researchers identify meaningful relationships, recognize evidence gaps, and ask better questions.
     As human space exploration advances, understanding combustion beyond Earth's gravity is essential to informing future spacecraft fire-safety research. ARCAUS transforms complex NASA evidence into an engaging, transparent, and scientifically grounded research experience.
details:
ARCAUS — Fire Beyond Gravity is an interactive scientific research observatory developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data.

What I developed: I built a web-based research platform that transforms NASA's microgravity combustion studies into an explorable collection of experiments, scientific findings, interactive visualizations, and source-linked comparisons. ARCAUS brings together research from BASS-II, Saffire-V, and SoFIE-GEL, helping users examine how airflow, oxygen concentration, material thickness, and fuel geometry influence flame behavior.

How it works: The platform organizes 31 curated findings, five cross-study comparisons, and verified BASS-II experimental records. Researchers can explore 18 PMMA test runs, inspect flame-spread measurements, examine 27 fabric ignition and extinction outcomes, and navigate visual experiment exhibits. Each comparison preserves experimental conditions and distinguishes verified measurements, published author conclusions, and hypotheses. I also developed a research API with searchable and ranked evidence retrieval and a Google Gemini integration designed to generate source-grounded explanations.

Technology: ARCAUS was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python-based scientific data analysis, structured JSON, GitHub, and Cloudflare for hosting and research infrastructure. Google Gemini API integration supports the AI research-assistant component. I used AI-assisted development tools for implementation and original illustrative artwork, while retaining responsibility for research direction, validation, design decisions, and interpretation.

Scientific findings: In the BASS-II PMMA data, I examined 18 independent test-run means and found a Spearman correlation of −0.718 between material thickness and measured flame-spread rate. I also compared published findings on ventilation changes, identifying why results from BASS-II and Saffire-V cannot be treated as universal fire-extinction rules.

What makes ARCAUS different: Rather than presenting disconnected papers or generating unsupported predictions, ARCAUS combines scientific traceability with an immersive visual interface. Users can move from a research question to relevant observations, experimental conditions, original NASA sources, and limitations.

Intended impact: ARCAUS aims to make microgravity combustion evidence easier to discover, compare, and communicate for researchers, engineers, students, and future space-exploration teams. It supports evidence-informed questions about spacecraft fire safety without claiming to establish operating thresholds or predict fire behavior on the Moon or Mars.

Considerations: Throughout development, I prioritized scientific accuracy, accessibility, source attribution, study independence, transparent uncertainty, and responsible AI use. ARCAUS is an independent project and is not an official NASA service.
